title: Language and Postcards
premise: Ansel Eriksen has spent twenty years mailing postcards to the house that burned down in 1999, a private ritual of correspondence with his dead mother and a family that scattered rather than speak. When the surviving Eriksen property—the childhood home where his father ruled through silence and selective memory—goes up for auction, Ansel is forced back into contact with his siblings, each of whom built an identity on a different version of their father. As the auction date approaches, Ansel discovers letters proving his father forged the will that disinherited their mother, and that his siblings have known longer than he has. The novel ends at the auction itself, where Ansel, instead of bidding, reads one of his unsent postcards aloud, shattering the family's arrangement of convenient silence and walking out owning nothing but his own language at last.
about_author: Sebastian Whitlock is the pen name of a former archivist who spent a decade cataloguing undeliverable mail in a northern postal depot. His fiction is known for its quiet obsession with what families say by refusing to say anything at all.

chapters.title: The Tenant
chapters.summary: Ansel's POV. We meet him writing his weekly postcard to a burned address, living in a rented room he never unpacks, working a job he describes as temporary after fifteen years. The beat is the eerie comfort of impermanence—until a certified letter arrives: the Eriksen house is going to auction, and he is named in the estate papers.

chapters.title: Certified Mail
chapters.summary: Ansel travels to his hometown for the estate reading, narrating the train ride as a return to a country that no longer exists. His brother Tomas greets him with practiced warmth; his sister Maren refuses to come at all. The beat is dread disguised as obligation, and the first hint that the siblings' politeness is load-bearing.

chapters.title: What the House Remembers
chapters.summary: Ansel walks the empty house alone before the auction, rooms triggering memories of his father's controlled silences and his mother's exile to the garden room. He finds his old postcards returned to sender, unopened, stacked in a drawer. The beat is grief surfacing as inventory—he is cataloguing his childhood like evidence.

chapters.title: Maren's Version
chapters.summary: Maren's POV, a flashback chapter. She recounts the winter their mother was sent away and the story the family agreed to tell instead. Maren stayed to watch her father, believing vigilance was love. The beat is the corrosion of a daughter who mistook witnessing for power, and who now wants the house burned symbolically, if not literally.

chapters.title: Tomas the Heir
chapters.summary: Tomas's POV. The eldest, he inherited the father's role and the father's debts, and has quietly arranged the auction with a buyer who will erase the house entirely. He believes erasure is mercy. The beat is power repeating itself: Tomas is becoming the man he hated, and knows it, and proceeds anyway.

chapters.title: The Garden Room
chapters.summary: Ansel, searching the house for his mother's belongings before the sale, finds a locked box in the garden room wall: her unsent letters to him, and a copy of the original will. The beat is revelation as violation—the discovery that his postcard ritual was answered all along, by a mother he could have found.

chapters.title: The Forged Hand
chapters.summary: Ansel confronts Tomas with the will; Tomas admits he has known for years and chose stability over truth, because the lie is the only thing holding his own family together. Maren arrives uninvited, and the three siblings fight in the kitchen where their father once ended arguments by leaving the room. The beat is the family's arrangement breaking apart in real time.

chapters.title: Postcards to the Living
chapters.summary: Ansel's POV. He spends the night before the auction writing postcards to each living Eriksen—honest ones, the kind he never sent. He visits the ruins of the burned house and, for the first time, reads a card aloud to the air instead of mailing it. The beat is the shift from correspondence as avoidance to language as confrontation.

chapters.title: The Auction
chapters.summary: The auction room, all three siblings present, buyers circling the lot. When the house comes up, Ansel stands and instead of bidding reads his mother's final unsent letter aloud—the forgery named, the silence named, Tomas named. The beat is public rupture: the family myth collapses in front of strangers, and the hammer falls on a house no one wants anymore.

chapters.title: Return to Sender
chapters.summary: Weeks later. The house sells cheap to a stranger who will never know what happened in it. Ansel mails one last postcard—to his mother's old address, now a real deliverable place—and receives, impossibly, a note back from the new tenant. Maren writes to him for the first time in years. The beat is quiet, earned resolution: inheritance refused, identity claimed, language finally addressed to the living.
